overview.summary: Software engineers design, build, test and maintain the programs and systems behind websites, apps and digital tools.
overview.problems: They turn real needs, such as booking a ticket, paying a bill or tracking a delivery, into reliable software that people can use.
overview.worksWith: Other engineers, designers, product managers and testers, and in small teams sometimes directly with customers or business owners.
overview.workplaces: Technology companies, banks, hospitals, government bodies, start-ups, and freelance or remote work.

timeline.title: Team check-in and planning
timeline.description: The team shares what each person finished, what they plan to do today and where they are stuck. The engineer chooses the first task of the day.
timeline.why: Short check-ins stop people repeating work and bring problems to the surface early.

timeline.title: Writing new code
timeline.description: The engineer builds a feature in small pieces and runs the code often to see whether it behaves as expected.
timeline.why: Clear, readable code is the main thing the role produces, and other people must be able to understand it later.

timeline.title: Testing and fixing bugs
timeline.description: The engineer writes tests, reproduces a reported problem, searches for its cause and fixes it.
timeline.why: A bug found before release costs far less to fix than one found by users.

timeline.title: Code review
timeline.description: The engineer reads a teammate's changes and leaves suggestions, and receives feedback on their own work.
timeline.why: Reviews catch mistakes and spread knowledge across the team.

timeline.title: Meetings, notes and learning
timeline.description: The engineer joins a planning or design discussion, writes notes explaining how something works, and reads about a tool needed for upcoming work.
timeline.why: Software lasts for years and tools change quickly, so clear notes and steady learning matter.

timeline.title: Urgent problems and on-call duty
timeline.description: In some teams, engineers take turns to respond when a live system fails, which can happen outside normal hours.
timeline.why: Many services must stay available at all times.

responsibilities: Writing and testing code that meets the needs of users
Finding and fixing bugs and slow or unreliable parts of a system
Reviewing teammates' work and welcoming review of their own
Documenting how systems work so others can maintain them
Estimating how long tasks take and telling the team early if something slips
Thinking about security and the privacy of user data
challenges: Much of the job is reading and understanding code that someone else wrote, not writing new code.
Some bugs are hard to reproduce and can take hours or days to find.
Deadlines and changing requirements can make plans shift quickly.
Tools and methods keep changing, so learning never stops.
Long hours at a screen call for deliberate breaks and healthy habits.
Some jobs include on-call duty at night or at weekends.
workEnvironment: Mostly desk and computer based, in offices, from home or a mix of both. Work is usually done in teams with regular meetings. Hours are often regular, but deadlines or on-call duty can mean evenings or weekends in some jobs.
rewards: Seeing something you built used by real people
Many industries and problems to choose from
Skills that can be practised and shown through projects
Some employers offer flexible or remote work
tradeoffs: Long focus time on screens, with a lot of reading and debugging
Learning that sometimes continues outside working hours
Job availability and pay vary by country, employer and experience

activity.title: Build a one-page website about something you like
steps: Choose a topic you enjoy, such as a hobby or a favourite sport.
Follow a free beginner HTML lesson, for example on freeCodeCamp or MDN Web Docs, and create a page with a heading, a paragraph and an image.
Add one small change, such as a new colour or a link to another page.
Break something on purpose, for example by removing a closing tag, see what happens, then fix it.
Write down which parts felt enjoyable and which felt frustrating.
activity.outcome: You experience a small version of the build, test and fix cycle and learn whether it feels interesting to you.
activity.safety: Use only your own text and images, and do not publish personal details online.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
